/docs/fluid-signals/.title: Fluid Signals API
/docs/fluid-signals/.content:
This page documents the API of fluid.cell, the primitive of the reactive library underlying Fluid Infusion 6. You can read background information on how fluid.cell offers extra capabilities above traditional reactive libraries, and also a more extended essay explaining its goals in the context of a malleable substrate.

The raw markdown underlying these docs is available on GitHub, suitable for direct ingestion by your friendly local neighbourhood intelligence.

Some examples on this page are live - complete and self-contained, they can be edited, and are run once they are free of errors: what each logs appears in the console beneath it. The other examples show syntax alone, e.g. a fragment of a layer record, and are read-only. Every example is checked by Infusion’s linter, down to the interiors of its references and directives as Infusion reads them - hover over a marked error to see what is wrong, and, for an editable example, a fix.

Construction

fluid.cell(initialValue, props)

  • {Any} [initialValue] - The initial value to store in the cell
  • {Object} [props] - Optional additional properties to contextualise the cell
  • Returns: {Cell} - The freshly constructed cell

A fresh reactive cell is constructed, with an optional initial value and optional additional properties.

If the initial value is undefined, this will be upgraded to an unavailable value marking the signal’s value as uninitialised.

The supported properties in props are

  • {String} name - Supplies a name or address for this cell, reported by fluid.cell.explain and fluid.cell.findCause. Cells allocated by the framework are named by the convention <role> for path <component path>, e.g. potentia for path story-6.lostPlants
  • {Function} equiv - A policy (oldValue, newValue) => Boolean deciding when an update leaves the cell’s value morally unchanged. If it finds the new value equivalent to the old, the cell keeps the value it held and notifies nothing downstream. It is consulted only when both values are available - otherwise, and for a cell without one, values are compared by fluid.cell.equals. fluid.cell.isEquivalent(cell, oldValue, newValue) applies a cell’s policy. Two policies are supplied:
    • fluid.equiv.elementwise - Arrays of the same length holding identical elements in the same order, or plain objects with the same keys holding identical values, are equivalent - e.g. a list of components assembled afresh
    • fluid.equiv.byKey(keyOf) - Values are equivalent if identical, or if keyOf returns the same key for each

Reading and writing

Cell.get()

The value of a reactive cell can be read by calling Cell.get. This forces the reactive tree of computations behind the cell to bring its value up to date. A call to Cell.get of some cell within the reactive context of a computed function (that is, further up its call stack) will set up an automatic subscription of the function to updates of that cell, rerunning the function whenever the value changes. If a further invocation of the computed does not execute Cell.get for that cell, the dynamic subscription will be torn down.

To read a cell within a computation without subscribing to it, read it within fluid.cell.untracked.

Cell.set(newValue, [options])

  • {any} newValue The new value to which the cell is to be updated
  • {String|Object} [options] Either a source tag to be applied to this update as it propagates, or an object holding any of
    • {Any} source - The source tag
    • {String} cause - Why the write was made, recorded for diagnostics alone and reported by fluid.cell.explain. Unlike a source, it takes no part in propagation

The reactive cell’s value can be updated by calling Cell.set. This will trigger a cascade of updates through the reactive tree. Any computed values that are depended on by effects will be marked to execute when fluid.cell.stabilize is next called. Computed values that are not depended on by effects will only be updated if Cell.get is called for a cell which depends on them.

Optionally, at the time of calling Cell.set, the reactive update can be marked with a source, which encodes the identity of the source in the world triggering the change. A source is usually a string, but may be any value compared by identity, e.g. the self source of a component returned by fluid.selfSource. An effect marked with a matching source in its excludeSource will skip notification. This scheme allows the reactive graph to avoid cyclically propagating changes back to the same source which triggered them. The second example after fluid.effect shows this source tracking facility in action.

A source travels with the update through every computed value which depends on the cell, and also through effects. Any cell which an effect sets whilst it runs is updated with the sources of the change which caused the effect to run, as well as any source of its own. A change caused by a source therefore remains marked with it however many effects it passes through - see FLUID-5498. It is also carried across an asynchronous computation. Its eventual value, once it settles, reaches its dependents still marked with the sources of the change which started it. Within an effect, this holds only for cells set synchronously by the effect’s function, not for any set later, e.g. after an await.

Each fresh change to a cell from outside the reactive graph carries only its own sources. The sources of an earlier change don’t linger on the cell, even while an asynchronous effect that the earlier change triggered is still pending.

Sources can also be applied to every cell set within a function by wrapping it with fluid.cell.withAmbientSource(source, fn), where source is a source or an array of them. This returns a function suitable for use as an event listener. Calls may be nested, and a cell set within them carries the sources of each.

Cell._value

A “blind read” of the current value of the cell, regardless of how stale it is, can be made by looking at the _value property. This isn’t recommended except in specialised cases, usually of framework-building.

Relations and effects

Cell.computed(fn, staticSources, props)

  • {Function | null} fn - The function which will reactively evaluate this cell’s value, or null if an existing relation is to be torn down
  • {Cell[]} [staticSources] - Any statically known cell dependencies whose reactively evaluated arguments will be supplied to fn when it is called
  • {ComputedProps} [props] - Optional additional properties to contextualise the computation
  • Returns: {Cell} - This cell

computed is available as a function in the prototype of cells created via fluid.cell.

Cell.computed constructs or tears down a computed relationship between a target cell (this one) and one or more source cells accepted by the supplied function fn. The function will be invoked when the pull of a reactive value via Cell.get or an effect demands the value of the target cell and the values of one or more of the source cells have changed. The function will be invoked with arguments formed by evaluating the values of the source cells supplied in staticSources.

As well as the source cells supplied in staticSources, any other cells that the function references as it executes will also be tracked and schedule a reinvocation of the function, following the standard tracking semantics of commodity signals implementations.

If any of the source cells evaluates to an unavailable value, invocation of fn will be short-circuited and upstream cells will receive a corresponding, perhaps wrapped, unavailable value directly.

The first staticSource cell, if there is one, will have a special status of establishing the key of the relationship which will be unique in the context of the target cell. If there is no such cell, a null value will serve as the key. If an existing relation is present on the target cell with the same key, it will be replaced by the supplied one.

If null is supplied in place of the fn argument, any existing relation with the same key will be torn down.

The additional ComputedProps argument can contain the following fields:

{Object} ComputedProps:

  • {Boolean} isFree - Indicates if this is a “free” computation that will deliver unavailable values.

Here is a basic example setting up two cells connected by a simple computation:

For a more advanced example setting up and tearing down bidirectional relationships, you can see the visual test sample for Bidirectional temperature conversion in the extended essay.

Asynchronous computations

A computation set up by Cell.computed may be asynchronous. If its function returns, rather than a plain value, either:

  • A Promise representing a deferred value or error, or
  • An AsyncIterator, e.g. as returned by an async generator function, representing a bounded or unbounded sequence of deferred values,

the cell holds a pending value until the promise settles, or until the first value is yielded, and then the value it resolves to or yields. A promise which rejects leaves the cell holding an unavailable value reporting the error. Computations which depend on the cell are not run with the promise, but once its value is available.

Whether a computation is asynchronous is discovered from what its function returns, and so no declaration is needed - an async function, and a plain function which returns a promise, are treated alike. Once a computation has returned a promise or async iterator, its cell is marked pending from the outset of each later run.

Here’s an example receiving a result through an asynchronous computation. Rather than manually waiting for event turns as here, asynchronous results are more conveniently received through fluid.cell.signalToPromise, see below.

fluid.cell.effect(fn, [staticSources], [props])

  • {Function} fn - The function to execute reactively when any of the staticSources change

  • {Cell[]} staticSources - The array of source cells whose values are dependencies for the effect

  • {Object} [props] - Optional properties to configure the effect

  • {Function} [props.onDispose] - Optional cleanup function to run when the effect is disposed

  • {Boolean} [props.isFree] - If true, the effect will run even if some sources are unavailable, delivering unavailable values in their place.

  • {any} [props.excludeSource] - If this optional field is populated, a change triggered by Cell.set whose source (supplied as the source argument there) matches this value will skip notifying this effect.

  • {any} [props.includeSource] - If this optional field is populated, only a change whose source matches this value will notify this effect.

  • Returns: {Effect}

fluid.cell.effect accepts a function and arguments to run when one or more reactive values change. The signature is similar to Cell.compute only an effect’s fn is expected to have some side-effect upon the world, such as printing a value or writing to a database, rather than computing a value internal to the reactive graph. Values returned from fn are ignored.

Effects do not activate automatically. Every effect cell is specially marked to be activated by fluid.cell.stabilize which will then pull reactive values through the graph and activate their fn if any of their reactive arguments have changed as a result.

Similarly to Cell.compute, if any cells referenced in staticSources or in dynamically tracked reactive values resolve to an unavailable value, and the effect is not marked as isFree, notification of the function is skipped.

In order to deactivate the effect it needs to be explicitly disposed by calling the Effect.dispose() method on the returned Effect. An effect represents a resource in the world outside the reactive graph and as such may require special actions when it is torn down. The optional props argument accepts a callback onDispose which is called when the effect is disposed via Effect.dispose().

This simple example follows the pattern of previous examples, but actively pulls updates to B using an effect rather than manually pulling them via get():

This example shows fluid.cell’s source tracking facility. If a source of changes is tagged by using the source argument to Cell.set, changes due to this source can skip notifying an effect with a matching excludeSource argument. This can be helpful when interfacing with external systems which should not be notified of changes that they themselves have caused:

An effect which is skipped - because its arguments are unchanged, or through includeSource or excludeSource - keeps observing every cell it read dynamically when it last ran, and still waits on any of them which is pending. An effect downstream of an asynchronous computation therefore sees it settle even if it was skipped meanwhile.

fluid.cell.stabilize()

fluid.cell.stabilize will run all effects whose reactive arguments have changed, after pulling updates through the reactive graph. Example code is in the section on effects.

Unlike in many reactive frameworks, effects do not run eagerly or synchronously — this choice is motivated in the deferred stabilization posting.

fluid.cell.stabilizeAsync()

A helpful utility layered on top of fluid.cell.stabilize which as well as scheduling any effects, will also return a promise which may be awaited, to be notified when any asynchronous computations launched by the stabilization operation have successfully notified the effects which depend on them.

Comprehension

When something updates, re-renders or turns over unexpectedly, ask the graph why before instrumenting it.

fluid.cell.explain([cell])

  • {Cell} [cell] The cell whose last change is to be explained. If absent, the cell whose update is in progress is used, so that it may be called from within a computation or effect
  • Returns: {String[]} The descriptions of the cells along the whole chain of cause, starting with cell, or an empty array if there is no target

This is the first tool to reach for. It follows the chain reported by fluid.cell.findCause back to the cell whose change began the reaction. Where that cell was given its value by set, it reports why - the cause and sources supplied to Cell.set - and continues from the update during which it was set, e.g. the effect which wrote it. The chain therefore reaches back past each write to what provoked it:

Pass {cause: "..."} to Cell.set in your own code to make its writes explain themselves.

fluid.cell.findAllCauses()

Gathers the causes of each source of the reaction in progress.

fluid.cell.pendingEffects()

  • Returns: {Cell[]} The effects holding the graph unsettled, e.g. those awaiting I/O or an asynchronous computation - the outstanding work for which fluid.cell.settle waits

Profiling

To profile, or to find when events happen, wrap fluid.cell.update in the page and filter on cell.name, masking instance numbers (/\d+/g) to aggregate.

fluid.cell.findCause([cell])

  • {Cell} cell If supplied, the cell whose update cause should be reported. If absent, any current reaction will be used instead.
  • Returns: {Cell[]}

Reports the cause of any reaction which has updated a given cell, or else the one that is currently in progress, in the form of an array of nodes reaching back from the supplied cell to the one whose modification triggered the reaction. The triggering cell appears first in the array.

Utilities

fluid.cell.signalToPromise(valSignal)

  • {Cell<any>} valSignal - The signal to monitor.
  • Returns: Promise<any> - A Promise that resolves with the signal’s first available value.

Gear from the world of signals into a Promise that can be awaited.

The asynchronous computation example from above is more conveniently written:

Cell.refresh(staticSources)

  • {Cell[]} [staticSources] - An optional array of static source cells to identify the computation edge to be refreshed
  • this: {Cell} The cell for which an incoming edge is to be refreshed

A method available on any Cell: Refreshes the value of the cell by re-evaluating its computation for the specified static sources. Finds the incoming edge corresponding to the given static sources and triggers an update for this cell along that edge. Particularly useful when the value is computed via an asynchronous activity in the world — if the edge is async, the cell’s value will be set to stale and the asynchronous activity will be restarted.

fluid.cell.untracked(fn)

  • {Function} fn - The function to execute without tracking
  • Returns: {any} - The value returned by fn

Executes a function, within a computation or effect, without subscribing the computation to any cell which the function reads. This suits a value which is consulted rather than depended upon. For example, an effect which closes a popup on a press outside it should read whether the popup is open, but should not rerun when it is opened, since opening it is no reason to look again at a press made before it was opened:

untracked is needed whenever an effect reads a value which it also writes, for example an effect which appends to a history:

Without it, the effect depends on history, so each write reruns it, and it would append forever. An effect which keeps triggering itself like this is stopped after fluid.cell.maxEffectRuns (100) runs within one stabilization, and is reported, naming the effect, through fluid.cell.reportCycle, which logs to console.error. In the Integration Language this is rarely needed, since a $method runs untracked - an effect which updates such values by calling a method needs no untracked of its own.

Unavailable values

Some background on unavailable values is available on their own page. An unavailable value held at a cell represents a value which is either uninitialised, pending due to outstanding I/O, or an error.

Unavailable values can be received by effects by marking them with the isFree property — otherwise, they only receive fully settled, concrete values.

An unavailable value is created using the fluid.unavailable API, which in the simplest usage simply accepts a string holding a message explaining why the value is unavailable. These values are normally created by frameworks rather than users.

fluid.unavailable(cause = {}, variety = “error”)

  • {String|Object|Array} [cause={}] - A list of dependencies or reasons for unavailability.
  • {String} [variety="error"] - The variety of unavailable value:
    • "error" indicates a syntax issue that needs design intervention.
    • "config" indicates that an expected value has been configured away or is missing - the value may appear through regular user action
    • "pending" indicates the value depends on pending I/O which is expected to imminently resolve
  • Returns: {Unavailable} An unavailable value marker.

A special variety of unavailable value represents a value which is temporarily stale as a result of I/O pending to update it. This is created by fluid.pending which is just a wrapper for fluid.unavailable:

fluid.pending(staleValue, site)

  • {Any} staleValue - The most recently seen value before it became unavailable due to pending I/O.
  • {String} site - The site or resource (e.g. URL) responsible for the pending I/O.
  • Returns: {Unavailable} An object representing the unavailable state due to pending I/O.

fluid.isUnavailable(totest)

  • {any} totest - The value to be tested for being an unavailable value
  • Returns {Boolean} true if the supplied value was an unavailable, false if it is a plain value.

For more complex examples of propagating and receiving unavailable states, please consult the test cases in GitHub, and in this context, “Error propagation across async graph”, “Error propagation across async surfacing as promise rejection”.

/docs/fluid-signals-background/.title: Fluid Signals background
/docs/fluid-signals-background/.content:
This page contains background information motivating the design of fluid.cell, the reactive primitive built to support Infusion 6, explaining how it differs from traditional reactive libraries. There are also API docs for fluid.cell and also a more extended essay explaining its goals in the context of a malleable substrate.

I chose the name “cell”, rather than “signal” which is more common in the 2020s JavaScript reactive community, in honour of 3 traditions:

  • Spreadsheet cells, which are the public’s primeval grounding in reactivity.
  • Kenny Tilton’s Cells system for CLOS, which in 2001, 5 years before the coining of the terms “glitch” and “reactive programming”, had already solved all the problems of reactivity embedded in imperative programming languages.
  • The notion of a reference cell in JavaScript and and other functional languages, taking the form of an object + key or 1-element array which mocks up the mutable capability of a pointer in languages which lack them.

There is now a consensus notion of the capabilities of a reactive library in JavaScript, amongst such popular implementations as preact-signals, alien-signals, Angular signals, Solid signal, etc. which has led to the proposal of a standardised JS implementation by the TC39 committee. This consensus baseline is often called “commodity signals” in pages on this site.

Whilst the core implementation of fluid.cell is consistent with this consensus implementation — in fact, it has been adopted directly from Milo Mighdoll’s amazing and minimal reactively system — this implementation departs from the consensus in some significant ways. These departures mostly widen the domain of validity of the implementation, relaxing restrictions which are incompatible with the demands of a substrate supporting malleable programming.

Whilst its idiom and goals are aligned with support for the Infusion 6 substrate, fluid.cell is a self-contained library with no dependencies which could be adopted for other purposes.

You can read its test cases here and run them here.

The best guide to reactive programming in general and fluid.cell’s algorithm in particular is Milo’s 2022 Super Charging Fine-Grained Reactivity which contrasts a variety of implementations including Reactively’s, about 2/3 of the way down the page with the red and green squares, which I have adopted.

Extra capabilities in fluid.cell

Bidirectional relationships

The most significant ergonomic difference in fluid.cell is support for bidirectional relationships between cells, which supports democratic constructs such as lenses without recourse to gratuitous asymmetries such as writable computed relations.

Multiple inbound compute arcs

Support for bidirectional relationships entails support for multiple computed relations capable of updating the value of a single cell. This is a capability not found in any popular reactive library. In isolation, this capability might lead to the possibility for inconsistent or conflicting updates — however, fluid.cell follows the insight from Dan Ingall’s Fabrik system which recognizes “bidirectional dataflow connections as a shorthand for multiple paths of flow”. As one leg of a bidirectional relationship is activated, the reverse leg is removed from consideration for this reactive update cycle (this kind of cycle is named a “fit”), removing the chance for cyclic updates.

Static compute arguments

Tied in with support for lenses and multiple incoming arcs is fluid.cell’s support for static arguments to compute arcs. This is a significant departure from commodity signals, which pride themselves on automatic discovery of dependencies as code executes in the compute arc. In a substrate forming an integration domain this is unidiomatic since base language code should ideally have no power of reference to surrounding scopes, in accordance with the principle of interface hiding. However, the use of static arguments isn’t mandatory, standard dynamic tracked dependencies are available to be used either instead of or along with them, to aid experts in interoperating with established codebases.

Cycle diagnostics

Another difference is the treatment of cycles. Rather than being rejected outright with a base language exception, these can be configured to either resolve benignly through having the cycle broken by deferring a potentially cyclic update to a further task, or else to resolve to an unavailable value which accumulates the addresses of the nodes involved, producing a visible diagnostic in the substrate[coming soon].

Cause tracking

A hugely important ergonomic improvement is being able to report the cause of any ongoing reaction, that is, the chain of updated nodes leading back to the initial changed node triggered by the user or environment. This is vital in a substrate which positions reactivity as a wholesale replacement for execution, and therefore needs to replace the invaluable explanatory power of the stack with a correspondingly thorough explanation stretching across the substrate. This is done with the fluid.findCause API which returns this path of updated nodes.

Asynchronous compute arcs

Finally, fluid.cell supports compute arcs which produce their results asynchronously. Whilst this is uncommon in reactive libraries, there is precedent for this in Ryan Carniato’s Solid signals supporting the upcoming 2.0 release of Solid, and Mike Bostock’s Runtime which powers Observable. fluid.cell passes the test cases (as of Nov 2025) issued for Solid signals’ createAsync.

/docs/fluid-ptf/.title: Potentia Transmission Format
/docs/fluid-ptf/.content:
This page documents the Potentia Transmission Format (PTF), a plain-text document format which captures everything required to reconstruct a live Fluid Infusion 6 component somewhere else: in another page, another application or another user’s session. It is implemented in FluidPTF.js. It transmits a component’s layers, its potentia and the contents of its live layer.

The raw markdown underlying these docs is available on GitHub, suitable for direct ingestion by your friendly local neighbourhood intelligence.

Some examples on this page are live - complete and self-contained, they can be edited, and are run once they are free of errors: what each logs appears in the console beneath it. The other examples show syntax alone, e.g. a fragment of a layer record, and are read-only. Every example is checked by Infusion’s linter, down to the interiors of its references and directives as Infusion reads them - hover over a marked error to see what is wrong, and, for an editable example, a fix.

Intention

A user should be able to point at any visible instance, choose “Copy”, and paste a working replica elsewhere, together with the state it had accumulated.

The format is designed to be:

  • Intelligible and hackable. A PTF document is ordinary text that can be read, diffed, edited in any text editor, pasted into a chat or an email, or written by hand.
  • Built on an existing standard. The container is MIME multipart (RFC 1341, RFC 2046), the format of email attachments. Each part carries a Content-Type and a filename, so that layers travel in their native representation: an SFC as .vue source, a JavaScript layer as JavaScript, live state as JSON.
  • Complete but minimal. It carries exactly the layers that are not part of the framework, and only the state that the user actually supplied or changed.

An example

Take the counter from Fluid View, loaded from my-counter.vue, rendered and clicked three times:

This is the complete document produced:

MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: multipart/mixed; boundary="ptf-boundary-buednuutq8"

This is a Potentia Transmission Format (PTF) document holding the layers and potentia of an Infusion component.
--ptf-boundary-buednuutq8
Content-Type: text/x-vue; charset=utf-8
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="my.counter"
Content-Description: layer

<script>
fluid.def("my.counter", {
    count: 0,
    increment: {
        $method: {
            func: self => self.count++,
            args: "{self}"
        }
    }
});
</script>

<template>
    <div class="counter">
        <span>Clicked @{count} times</span>
        <button @onclick="{self}.increment()">+1</button>
    </div>
</template>

<style>
.counter {
    display: flex;
    gap: 12px;
}
</style>

--ptf-boundary-buednuutq8
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="/"
Content-Description: potentia

{
    "$layers": [
        "my.counter"
    ]
}
--ptf-boundary-buednuutq8
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="/"
Content-Description: live

{
    "count": 3
}
--ptf-boundary-buednuutq8--

Reading it from the top:

  1. The MIME header declares a multipart document and its boundary string. The boundary is chosen at random so that it doesn’t occur in any part.
  2. The preamble line is ignored by decoders, but tells a human reader what they are looking at.
  3. The layer part is the SFC exactly as its author wrote it.
  4. The potentia part for / says the component was made from my.counter. Its container argument has been dropped, because it was a DOM node.
  5. The live part for / records that count was changed to 3.

Pasting this into another page and calling fluid.ptf.instantiate(text, {potentia: {container}}) renders “Clicked 3 times”, and the copy then counts on from 3 independently of the original.

With a JavaScript layer and a subcomponent

If the counter is embedded in a panel defined in plain JavaScript:

then the document holds these parts:

Kind Filename Content type Body
layer my.counterPanel text/javascript The fluid.def("my.counterPanel", {...}); call, regenerated from the stored definition
layer my.counter text/x-vue The SFC source, as above
potentia / application/json {"$layers": ["my.counterPanel"], "title": "Visitor clicks"}
live /counter application/json {"count": 2}

There is no potentia part for /counter, because the panel’s layer creates the counter itself. Its live state is still sent, keyed by its path.

Transmitting components, not data

Conventional copy and paste moves data in an application-specific format: text, an image, a spreadsheet range, or a serialised blob. Sender and receiver must agree in advance on what that data means, and the receiver must already contain the code that gives it behaviour. A rich clipboard flavour only works between applications that share an understanding of it, and what moves is always the application’s output, never a piece of the application itself.

PTF is a single, general format, which a receiver needs to understand only once. What it carries is a component of the application itself: the definitions that produce it, not data shaped for a particular consumer. Because an Infusion component is fully determined by its layers plus a small record of how it was configured and changed, sending those is enough to rebuild it, with its behaviour intact. The receiver doesn’t need to have seen the component, or any application like it, before.

Preserving authorship

A component is not built from one block of code but from a stack of layers, often written by different people at different times. A base layer from a library, a derived layer from an application author, a $linkage contributed by a plugin, the user’s own configuration and the edits made during use are each a separate contribution, merged by the framework with well-defined precedence.

PTF keeps that structure. Each layer travels as its own part, under its own name, in the source format its author wrote it in: an SFC as the .vue file it was loaded from, verbatim, not regenerated. The user’s configuration and the live changes made during use travel separately again. A PTF document is never compiled, bundled or flattened into one tangled block of source code in which nobody can tell which lines came from whom.

This has consequences for the receiver:

  • Provenance is legible. Anyone reading the document can see which author contributed what, and in what order the contributions apply.
  • Contributions stay separable. A receiver can keep its own, perhaps newer, version of a library layer, and accept only the application author’s layer and the user’s state. It can also edit a single layer without disturbing the others.
  • The copy remains malleable. The rebuilt component has the same layered structure as the original, so it can be adapted, re-linked and transmitted onward in the same terms. Its history of authorship grows rather than being erased at each hop.

What is transmitted

A component’s merged contents come from three kinds of source, and each is transmitted as a separate kind of part, named in its Content-Description header:

Kind What it holds Filename Content type
layer The definition of each user layer resolved into the $layers of the component or any of its subcomponents The layer name text/x-vue, text/javascript or application/json
potentia The user potentia: the arguments supplied when the component was created (to its creator function or fluid.pushPotentia) The component’s path, e.g. / or /counter application/json
live The contents of the component’s live layer: every value written to it during its lifetime The component’s path application/json

The first kind is sometimes called “Potentia I” (the reusable definitions) and the other two “Potentia II” (what distinguishes this particular instance).

Details:

  • Which layers. Framework layers (those with $variety: "framework" or "frameworkAux") are omitted, since the receiver is expected to have its own copy of the framework. So are layers whose definitions can’t be found.
  • Layer representation. A layer loaded from a Single File Component is sent as its SFC source text, byte for byte, including its <template> and <style>. Any other layer is rendered as a fluid.def(...) call in JavaScript, with functions included by their source text. Live layers, whose names are rendered sites beginning with {, are JSON. fluid.layerMimeType(layerName) reports which representation a layer will use. SFC layers are recognised by the tag layer fluid.sfcLayer, which the SFC loader adds to every layer it loads.
  • Paths. Filenames for potentia and live parts are paths relative to the transmitted component, which is /. A subcomponent at member counter is /counter, and segments are URI-encoded.
  • Potentia of the root. The root’s potentia part always holds $layers, the full list of layers the component was created with. Its first entry is the layer whose creator function will rebuild it.
  • Live layer. This is flattened to a map from path to value, e.g. {"count": 3, "state.prompt": "Hi"}.
  • Values that can’t travel. Potentia and live values are reduced to what JSON can represent faithfully. Values supplied by the host environment, such as a container DOM node or a function, are dropped, and so is any object left empty by dropping them, e.g. a view record holding only a container. The receiver supplies its own.
  • Subcomponents. Subcomponents are visited recursively. A subcomponent created by a $component record in a layer needs no potentia part, because its layer recreates it, but its live state is still transmitted.

Reconstruction

fluid.ptf.instantiate(text, options) rebuilds the component in three steps:

  1. Register layers. Each layer part is registered. An SFC goes through fluid.loadSFCText, a JavaScript part is evaluated (running its fluid.def(...) call), and a JSON part is passed to fluid.def. A layer the receiver already defines is left alone unless overrideLayers is set.
  2. Construct the root. A free component is created from the root’s potentia part, with options.potentia merged over it, using the creator function of the first entry in its $layers. A document with no root potentia part is rejected.
  3. Apply the rest. Once the root becomes available, the potentia parts of subcomponents are pushed at their paths. Then each subcomponent’s live part is written into its live layer once that subcomponent becomes available. Parts whose path matches no component are returned as unresolved.

A host which must take responsibility for the component before it becomes available, such as a canvas which may destroy the shape hosting it while it is still loading, can split the steps: fluid.ptf.constructParts performs the first two and returns the component at once, and fluid.ptf.applyParts then performs the third.

Trust

Instantiating a PTF document runs the code in its layers. Its JavaScript parts are evaluated, and its SFCs’ scripts are executed. Accepting a PTF document therefore requires the same trust as loading an SFC or script from its source. Unless overrideLayers is set, a document can’t replace a layer the receiver already has, but it can define new ones.

Embedding PTF: the tldraw clipboard

PTF documents nest, and other kinds of part can travel alongside them. The tldraw integration (demo/tldraw/js/tldraw-clipboard.js) replaces tldraw’s own clipboard format, which is opaque and compressed, with a plain-text PTF document:

Kind Filename Body
tldraw tldraw-content tldraw’s own JSON for all copied shapes, native ones included, with their ids and positions
component A shape id A nested multipart/mixed entity holding that shape’s component parts

On paste, the clipboard text is checked with fluid.ptf.isPTF:

  • Plain text. If it isn’t a PTF document, tldraw handles the paste as normal.
  • Copied shapes. A document with a tldraw part is pasted through tldraw, so that ids are remapped and positions resolved as for a native paste. Each recreated Infusion shape is then rebuilt from its nested component parts.
  • A bare component. A document as produced by fluid.ptf.componentToPTF, for example one copied out of a text editor, becomes a single fresh shape.

Cut and undo use the same mechanism: before a shape is deleted, its component’s parts are captured, so that undoing the cut restores the component with the state it had.

Because the clipboard holds readable text, a copied component can be pasted into a text editor, modified there (for example by changing its template or its count) and pasted back onto the canvas as a modified component.

ZIP encoding

A widget may also travel as a ZIP file, e.g. one dropped onto a page being edited with Edit in Infusion. This suits a widget written as a set of files, by an author or an agent, rather than copied from a live instance. A ZIP file is the same PTF document spelled as files: each part becomes a file, and the receiver reads the files back into the parts that fluid.ptf.instantiateParts takes. A ZIP file may also simply hold a PTF document as a file ending .ptf.

Part File Example
layer A .vue, .js or .json file, named for the layer it defines, either at the top level or within layers/ energy-driver.vue, or layers/energy.driver.vue
potentia of the root components/potentia.json, which may be omitted for a driver {"$layers": ["energy.driver"]}
potentia of a subcomponent components/<member>/.../potentia.json components/counter/potentia.json
live components/[<member>/...]live.json components/live.json
An image img/<name>, or any image file, written to the site’s images as <name> img/cat.png

Files made by an archiver, such as __MACOSX/ and .DS_Store, are ignored.

Naming files for their layers

A layer’s file is named exactly as a site names it once the widget is published. The layer’s name has its dots replaced by hyphens, as for any SFC loaded through <fluid-import>. The layer energy.chartBase is therefore held in energy-chartBase.vue, and the name is case-sensitive. A file whose name already holds dots, such as layers/energy.chartBase.vue, is read as that layer’s name directly. A site finds a layer by its file’s name, so:

  • Each file defines the layer it is named for. An SFC may define further layers used only within it, for example the concrete charts its own template renders. Any layer which other files refer to needs a file of its own.
  • Every relative <fluid-import src> names a file in the ZIP. The widget’s files are written side by side into the site’s directory of SFCs, so an import such as <fluid-import src="./energy-chartBase.vue"> keeps working there.
  • No plain scripts. A .js file loaded by another file’s <script src> is not a layer, and a widget can’t yet carry one. Put its code in the <script> of the SFC which loads it, or make it a layer of its own. A script from outside the widget, such as a library loaded from a CDN by an absolute URL, is fine.

A ZIP file which breaks any of these rules is refused as a whole, with a message naming each file at fault and, where it can, the name the file should have. The check matters because the editor’s preview loads every file at once: a misnamed layer still renders there, and would fail only on the published site.

A reference to {self}.container is refused too, since it names nothing: a component’s element is {self}.view.container, and an effect waiting on what doesn’t exist silently never runs.

The driver

A PTF document always has a root potentia part, naming the layers the widget is made of. A ZIP file may leave out components/potentia.json when its root can be told from its files alone. The root is then made of a single layer, with no further potentia, which is the same as a components/potentia.json of {"$layers": ["<root layer>"]}. The root layer is:

  • the widget’s only layer, if it has just one; or else
  • its driver: the one layer which none of its other files refers to. A file refers to a layer by importing its file with <fluid-import src> or <script src>, or by its name as a string, e.g. in $layers or a fluid-layers attribute.

A ZIP file with several layers which no other file refers to, and no components/potentia.json, is refused. Name its root in components/potentia.json instead. Write components/potentia.json anyway whenever the root takes potentia of its own, such as a caption.

Checklist for writing a ZIP file

To write a widget as a ZIP file that a site will accept, for instance as an agent:

  1. Choose a namespace for the widget’s layers, e.g. energy, and give each layer a name within it, e.g. energy.chartBase.

  2. Write each layer as an SFC named for it: energy-chartBase.vue containing fluid.def("energy.chartBase", {...}), together with any <template> and <style> the layer has. A layer drawing into its own markup, e.g. with a charting library, does so in an effect taking the element as {self}.view.container. A component has no member container of its own, and an effect waiting on an argument that doesn’t exist silently never runs.

  3. Write the driver as an SFC which pulls in the others with <fluid-import src="./energy-chartBase.vue">, and lays out the widget in its <template>, placing each part of it by fluid-layers:

    <template>
<main class="energy-driver">
  <div fluid-layers="energy.historyChart"></div>
  <div fluid-layers="energy.extrapolatedChart" fluid-id="projection"></div>
</main>
</template>

    Each such element is a subcomponent of the driver, named by its fluid-id, or else by its first layer’s last segment - here historyChart and projection. Two elements of one template may not share a name, so give fluid-ids to two parts of the same layer. A part which other layers should be able to configure or remove with null is declared instead as a member of the driver’s layer, historyChart: {$component: {$layers: "energy.historyChart"}}, and placed by <div @id="historyChart"></div>. An element may not bear both.

  4. Fold any shared helper script into the <script> of the base SFC which needs it.

  5. Put any images in img/, and refer to them from templates as /img/<name>.

  6. Zip the files, with the layers at the top level, or under layers/ if you prefer. Add components/potentia.json only to give the root potentia of its own, or when there are several candidates for the driver.

For example:

energy-chart.zip
├── energy-chartBase.vue        defines energy.chartBase - the chart's spec, legend and layout, and the helpers
├── energy-chartSvg.vue         defines energy.chartSvg, on energy.chartBase - an SVG renderer
├── energy-chartChartJs.vue     defines energy.chartChartJs - a Chart.js renderer, loaded from a CDN
├── energy-dataHistory.vue      defines energy.dataHistory, on energy.chartBase - the data
└── energy-driver.vue           defines energy.driver - imports the four files above, and defines and lays out
                                energy.historyChart, as [energy.chartSvg, energy.dataHistory], placing
                                it by fluid-layers in its template

Here energy.driver is the root, since none of the other files refers to it.

JavaScript API

Producing documents

  • fluid.ptf.componentToPTF(component) returns {String}, the complete PTF document for component and its subcomponents.
  • fluid.ptf.componentToParts(component) returns {PTFPart[]}, the parts without encoding them. This is useful for embedding a component’s parts in a larger document.
  • fluid.ptf.encode(parts, [preamble]) returns {String}, encoding any parts as a PTF document. A part with parts in place of body is encoded as a nested multipart entity.
  • fluid.layerMimeType(layerName) returns {String}, the MIME type a layer will be transmitted in.

A PTFPart is {kind, contentType, filename, body}, or {kind, filename, parts} for a nested document. Decoded parts also carry headers, all of their headers with lower-cased names.

Reading documents

  • fluid.ptf.isPTF(text) returns {Boolean}: true if text begins with MIME-Version: and declares a multipart boundary. It is cheap enough to sniff every paste.
  • fluid.ptf.decode(text) returns {PTFPart[]|Unavailable}. It decodes nested multipart parts recursively, and returns an unavailable value if text is not a PTF document.
  • fluid.ptf.instantiate(text, [options]) returns {Promise<{that, unresolved}>} and runs reconstruction. Its options are:
    • options.potentia - Extra potentia merged over the root’s, e.g. {container}.
    • options.overrideLayers - If true, transmitted layers replace existing definitions.
  • fluid.ptf.instantiateParts(parts, [options]) does the same as instantiate, for parts that have already been decoded.
  • fluid.ptf.constructParts(parts, [options]) returns {Component}. It registers the layers and constructs the root component without waiting for it to become available, and applies none of the further parts. It throws if there is no root potentia part.
  • fluid.ptf.applyParts(that, parts) returns {Promise<String[]>}. It applies the subcomponent potentia and live parts to an existing component, and resolves with the filenames of any it could not place.
  • fluid.ptf.registerLayerParts(parts, [overrideLayers]) registers just the layer parts.
  • fluid.loadSFCText(layerName, text) registers an SFC from text rather than a URL. Reconstruction uses it for SFC parts.
